A1.justification: Despite the changed title, both PDFs describe Rep3D, with matching authors, architecture, core experiments, and substantial shared content. All pages, including figures, equations, tables, and appendices, support comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original segmentation experiments across five benchmark settings, ERF visualizations, and ablations of generator design, branch learning rates, and architectural integration.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds kernel-scaling experiments, convergence and runtime measurements, and comparisons with additional segmentation architectures.

M1.justification: The distance-based prior, two-layer depthwise modulation generator, multiplicative kernel re-parameterization, and plain encoder with 21×21×21 kernels remain unchanged. The revised title and additional optimizer analysis do not introduce a different algorithm.

E1.justification: The five task and modality settings otherwise match. However, KiTS19 in v1 Section 4 becomes KiTS21 in v2 Appendix A.3 while the case description, splits, targets, and scores remain unchanged. The PDFs do not establish whether this corrects a label or changes the underlying cohort.

E2.justification: v2 Appendix B.1 and Table 10 add evaluated comparisons with ResEnc nnU-Net, STU-Net-H, and MedNeXt across all five benchmarks. This substantially expands the contemporary comparator set; the original comparisons in Tables 1 and 2 remain.

E3.justification: The general hyperparameter table changes batch size from 2 to 1. The AMOS-CT inventory changes from 361 to 200 cases, while its 160/20/20 split remains unchanged. Added studies specify kernel sweeps, checkpoint and runtime measurements, and official baseline schedules, typically 1000 epochs. These are reported setting changes and additions, without evidence that the original experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds a systematic 3D UX-Net backbone-kernel sweep from 3×3×3 to 21×21×21 in Table 4 and checkpoint/runtime comparisons of vanilla, fixed-prior, and LRBM variants in Table 7. These substantially extend the optimization evidence beyond the retained generator-kernel, generator-depth, branch-learning-rate, and integration ablations.

E5.justification: Table 2 retains p<0.01 markers but removes v1's explicit identification of the paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test against all baselines. Table 1 retains that description. This reduces statistical reporting specificity for AMOS; neither version supplies seed counts, repeated-training uncertainty estimates, or confidence intervals.

E6.justification: Tables 4, 7, and 10 add substantial kernel-scaling, convergence/runtime, and comparative result sets. In the retained Table 2, UNesT-B's AMOS-MRI right-adrenal Dice changes from 0.852 to 0.691 and its mean from 0.854 to 0.843. Rep3D's original benchmark means and the other retained quantitative ablations remain unchanged; the additions are not version-to-version performance gains.

T1.justification: Appendix A.1 adds an Adam/AdamW extension through Equations 19–25, analyzing moment-normalization cancellation, padded branch superposition, and central versus peripheral update magnitudes. v1 contained the SGD-style derivation and empirical AdamW results, but no corresponding adaptive-optimizer derivation or update-direction assumption.

C1.justification: The main contribution list and the scope of the abstract and conclusion remain substantively equivalent: ERF-inspired learnable spatial re-parameterization, a plain large-kernel 3D architecture, and superior segmentation across five benchmark settings. The new title and supporting experiments do not redefine those contributions.

C2.justification: v2 Section 5.3 strengthens the interpretation from beneficial spatial modulation to an assertion that the plain architecture is inherently unstable and the learned prior is necessary for convergence. It also adds interpretations of kernel-scaling saturation and accuracy–runtime trade-offs. The existing memory-cost and resolution-related limitations remain substantially unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 adds total training times for the three variants—17.3, 15.5, and 17.5 hours—and training-schedule information for the new baselines. It revises the batch-size documentation. Most preprocessing, architecture, hardware, and hyperparameter details are retained or relocated, and the source-code access information is unchanged.

R1.justification: v2 adds MedNeXt and STU-Net references and an in-text Adam citation, while removing several earlier references, including TransUNet, CoTr, and LeViT-UNet. The literature discussion is refocused, but the central positioning around spatially adaptive optimization of large 3D kernels remains.

P1.justification: The title and abstract are revised, related work is reorganized into distinct architectural families, and the ablation narrative is extensively rewritten. Most experimental setup details move into a substantially reorganized appendix, changing the document's narrative structure beyond simple renumbering.

P2.justification: The main text changes from a single-column to a two-column layout, with substantially reformatted tables, captions, and figure placement. Three new tables display the added studies. Figures 1–3 retain their original visual content while being rescaled or repositioned.

improvement.justification: v2 adds useful contemporary comparisons, kernel-scaling evidence, and runtime measurements absent from v1. However, the new Vanilla Rep control is single-branch with SGD in Section 5.3 but parallel-branch with AdamW in Appendix A.5, undermining the claimed isolation of spatial modulation and necessity for convergence. The new Adam derivation also infers constructive updates from insufficiently specified non-orthogonality assumptions. These problems affect the central optimization argument, leaving the net quality benefit of the additional evidence uncertain.
